en: Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Malla country, arrived at Pāvā and stayed there in the Jalūkā forest grove.
Now at that time, between Pāpā and the eastern [city], and between Pāpā and the western [city], at a shrine that had arisen in that interval,
a new assembly hall had been recently built, recently completed, and recently occupied by no ascetic,
nor brahmin, nor Malla, nor Malla youth, nor anyone else who was a human being in the world.

The Mallas of Pāpā heard that the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Malla country, had arrived at Pāpā and was staying there in the Jalūkāvana grove. Then, it occurred to the Mallas who were practicing proper conduct: "In our Udbhūta shrine, a new assembly hall has recently been constructed, recently completed, and recently occupied by a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, a Malla, or a Malla youth."
or by anyone else in the world who has become human. May the Blessed One and the community of monks partake of it first;

having been partaken of first by the Blessed One and the community of monks, we shall have performed our duty and done what is beneficial, and having attained prosperity and gained our gain, we shall partake of it afterwards. That will be for our long-term benefit.
"For the sake of their welfare, benefit, and happiness.

Then the Mallas of Pāpā, gathering in groups and assemblies, departed from Pāpā and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times, and sat down to one side.

As the Pāpīyakas, the Mallas, were seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dharma. Then, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the Pāpīyaka Mallas in many ways with a discourse on the Dharma, the Blessed One became silent.

Then the Mallas of Pāpā, having rejoiced and delighted in the words spoken by the Blessed One, rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One,
addressed him as follows: "Between our [city] and the river Ācīrnavatī, between the eastern and western Pāvā, at the newly erected shrine, there is a new assembly hall."

"It has been prepared recently, finished recently, and occupied recently by no ascetic, brahmin, Malla, Malla youth, or anyone else who is a human being in this world. May the Blessed One be the first to partake of it, along with the community of monks.
Once it has been partaken of first by the Blessed One and the community of monks, we shall have performed our duty and accomplished what is wholesome."

"Having attained our rise and having obtained our gain, we shall thereafter enjoy them; that will be for our long-term welfare, benefit, and happiness. The Blessed One consented to the Mallans of Pāpīyakā by remaining silent.
Then the Mallas of Pāpā, understanding that the Blessed One had consented by his silence, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from his presence.

Then, during the remainder of that very day, the Mallas of Pāpā, having prepared the assembly hall with carts... and having hung up oil lamps and lit them, approached the place where the Blessed One was. Having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One.

Having circumambulated [the hall] three times and having bowed with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was, they said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, the new assembly hall has been prepared in every way, and water-jars have been set out and oil lamps have been raised. Now, Blessed One, it is time for whatever the Blessed One deems appropriate.
Then the Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks and preceded by the community of monks, went toward the Mallas of Pāpīyakā.

He went to the assembly hall. Having arrived, he washed his feet outside the assembly hall, entered the hall, surveyed the entire hall, and sat down leaning against the central pillar, facing the east.
The community of monks also washed their feet outside the assembly hall, entered the hall, surveyed the entire hall, and sat down leaning against the western wall.
Facing east with the Blessed One before them,

the Mallas of Pāpā washed their feet outside the assembly hall, entered the hall, surveyed the entire hall, and sat down against the eastern wall facing west, with the Blessed One and the community of monks before them.

Then the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the Mallas of Pāpā with a discourse on the Dharma. Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them in many ways with a discourse on the Dharma, he dismissed them.

"The first watch of the night has passed; now is the time for which you deem it fit. "So be it, Venerable Sir," the Mallas of Pāpā replied to the Blessed One. Rising from their seats, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from his presence.
Then the Blessed One, knowing that the Mallas of Pāpā had not long departed, addressed the venerable Śāriputra.

"May it be inspired in you, Śāriputra, to deliver a discourse on the Dharma for the monks. My back is aching; I shall therefore stretch it for a moment. The Venerable Śāriputra consented by remaining silent.
Then the Blessed One, having arranged his upper robe in four folds and placed his outer cloak (*saṃghāṭī*)—which possesses the qualities of a multitude—upon his head, [lay down].
He prepares his bed on his right side, placing one foot upon the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, with the perception of light and keeping in mind the thought of rising.
Then, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the monks:

The Nirgrantha Jñātiputra has passed away at Pāvā. Because of his death, the followers of the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra have become divided; they dwell as quarrelsome, contentious, disputatious, and fallen into conflict, saying:
"You do not understand this Dharma and Vinaya; I understand this Dharma and Vinaya! What is this Dharma and Vinaya?"
"You understand... what is consistent for me is inconsistent for you. What should have been said first, you said last;
what should have been said last, you said first. Your conduct is improper... "Withdraw your claim, sir, for the sake of release from the dispute.
Thus they dwell, striking one another with the power of their mouths.
Furthermore, those lay disciples of the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra who dwell in Pāpā, dressed in white garments, have also become disillusioned, repelled,
and alienated by the Nirgrantha Jñātiputras— now divided, fallen into dispute, engaged in quarreling, brawling, and contention— and have departed from the Dharma and Vinaya.
[We have fallen] from that which is poorly proclaimed, poorly understood, non-leaving, not leading to enlightenment, split, discordant, and without refuge.

But this Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is our Teacher; and this Dharma-Vinaya is well-proclaimed, well-understood, leading to leaving, leading to enlightenment, undivided, harmonious, and possessing a refuge—a Teacher.
And let us, being united, harmonious,

and living in mutual agreement, not dispute out of doubt so that this holy life may endure for a long time; that will be for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for its welfare.

For the welfare and happiness of gods and humans, O venerable ones, there is one Dharma taught by the Blessed One himself, having realized it through his own direct knowledge and perfect awakening: namely, that all sentient beings subsist upon nutriment. Therefore, let us remain united, harmonious, and in mutual accord.

We do not dispute for the sake of doubt, so that this holy life may endure for a long time; that will be for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.
Namely: all sentient beings abide in conditioned formations;
[therefore,] heedfulness regarding wholesome qualities. Intermediate summary verse:
Sentient beings subsist on nutriment; furthermore, they abide in conditioned formations. Heedfulness regarding wholesome phenomena is proclaimed as the one [quality] that stands alone.
"Venerable sirs, there are two things that the Blessed One, having personally realized and fully awakened to, has proclaimed:
namely, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Having come together, being in harmony and in agreement, we shall—just as before—[proclaim them] for the sake of gods and humans."
Namely: ignorance and craving for existence;
the view of existence and the view of non-existence;
and lack of shame and lack of dread.
2.5 Shame and dread of blame; 2.6 Harsh speech and association with evil friends;
2.7 Gentle speech and association with virtuous friends.
Skill in [recognizing] offenses and skill in the emergence from offenses;
skill in meditative attainments and skill in emerging from meditative attainments;
skill in the elements and skill in mental attention.
Mindfulness and clear comprehension;
the power of analytical reflection and the power of cultivation;
and straightforwardness and gentleness.
Patience and gentleness; friendliness and hospitality;
lack of restraint over the doors of the sense faculties and lack of moderation in eating.
Guarding the doors of the sense faculties and moderation in eating;
addiction to moral discipline and addiction to views;
failure in moral discipline and failure in views.
The perfection of ethical conduct and the perfection of view;
the purification of ethical conduct and the purification of view;
and the purification of view, as well as the systematic application of effort regarding what has been seen.
A sense of spiritual urgency regarding things that inspire urgency; for one who is thus stirred, right application;
lack of contentment with regard to wholesome qualities and non-remissness in application;
and calm abiding and insight.
Wisdom and liberation;
the knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising. Intermediate summary verse: … the third term, craving for existence, lack of shame, and shame …
Venerable sirs, there are three things proclaimed by the Blessed One, having himself directly known and fully awakened to them:
namely, the three types of misconduct—misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.
Having become united, harmonious, and in agreement, we shall [abstain from them], as previously described, for the sake of gods and humans.
Namely, the three types of good conduct: good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind.

(3.3) The three unwholesome roots: greed as an unwholesome root, hatred as an unwholesome root, and delusion as an unwholesome root. (3.4) The three wholesome roots: non-greed as a wholesome root, non-hatred as a wholesome root, and non-delusion as a wholesome root.

Wal_3.5 There are three unwholesome thoughts: the thought of sensual desire, the thought of ill will, and the thought of cruelty. Wal_3.6 There are three wholesome thoughts: the thought of renunciation, the thought of non-ill will, and the thought of non-cruelty.
Wal_3.7 There are three realms: the realm of sensual desire, the realm of ill will, and the realm of cruelty.
Wal_3.8 Three elements: the element of renunciation, the element of non-ill will, and the element of non-harming.
Wal_3.9 Three elements: the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. Wal_3.10 Three elements: the realm of form, the formless realm, and the element of cessation.
// Intermediate Summary Verse // ...

Wal_3.11 There are three types of craving: craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmatṛṣṇā*), craving for form (*rūpatṛṣṇā*), and craving for the formless (*ārūpyatṛṣṇā*). Wal_3.12 There are three types of craving: craving for form (*rūpatṛṣṇā*), craving for the formless (*ārūpyatṛṣṇā*), and craving for cessation (*nirodhatṛṣṇā*).

Wal_3.13 There are three outflows (*āsrava*): the outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*). Wal_3.14 There are three searches (*eṣaṇā*): the search for sensual pleasures (*kāmaiṣaṇā*), the search for existence (*bhavaiṣaṇā*), and the search for the holy life (*brahmacaryaiṣaṇā*).

Wal_3.15 There are three states of existence (*bhava*): existence in the realm of desire (*kāmabhava*), existence in the realm of form (*rūpabhava*), and existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyabhava*).
Wal_3.16 There are three masses of darkness: the mass of darkness of the past, the mass of darkness of the future, and the mass of darkness of the present.
Wal_3.17 There are three fears: the fear of illness, the fear of old age, and the fear of death.
Wal_3.18 There are three feelings: pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Wal_3.19 There are three kinds of suffering: the suffering of suffering, the suffering of conditioned formations, and the suffering of change.
Wal_3.20.a There are three types of conceit: the conceit "I am superior," the conceit "I am equal," and the conceit "I am inferior.
Wal_3.20.b // Summary verse //
There are three outflows, searches, and existences arising from thirst;
there are masses of darkness, fears, feelings, and various kinds of suffering.
Wal 3.21 There are three time periods: the past time period, the future time period, and the present time period.
Wal 3.22 There are three bases of discourse: the basis of discourse concerning the past, the basis of discourse concerning the future, and the basis of discourse concerning the present.
Wal 3.23 Matter is subsumed under matter in three categories: visible and resistant, invisible and resistant, and invisible and non-resistant.
Wal_3.24 There are three formations: the bodily formation, the vocal formation, and the mental formation.
Wal_3.25 There are three types of mind: the mind like a sore, the mind like lightning, and the mind like a diamond.
Wal_3.26 There are three kinds of persons: the person of downward-turned wisdom, the person of lap-like wisdom, and the person of broad wisdom.

Wal_3.27 There are three types of elders: the elder by birth, the elder by convention, and the elder by Dharma. Wal_3.28 There are three groups: the group fixed in falsehood, the group fixed in correctness, and the group that is undetermined.
Wal_3.29 There are three kinds of accusations: based on what has been seen, what has been heard, and what is suspected.
The Tathāgata has three things that need no protection—those which the Tathāgata does not conceal, thinking, "Lest others should find out about me. What are the three?
The Tathāgata’s bodily conduct is completely pure; there is no impurity in the Tathāgatas’ bodily conduct that the Tathāgata would conceal, thinking, "Lest others should find out about me."

The Tathāgata is one whose conduct of speech is completely pure; there is no impurity in the Tathāgatas’ conduct of speech that the Tathāgata would conceal, thinking, "Lest others should find out about me.

The Tathāgata is one whose conduct of mind is completely pure; there is no impurity in the Tathāgatas’ conduct of mind that the Tathāgata would conceal, thinking, "Lest others should find out about me."
They would not understand.
The summary verse (uddāna) is: Wal_3.30.3.b.
The time periods, discourse, and location; the conditioned factors, mind, and the person; the three types of elders, the heap, and exhortation; and also the non-guardings.

Wal_3.31 There are three fires: the fire of passion, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion. Wal_3.32 There are three fires: the offertorial fire (āhavanīya), the household fire (gārhapatya), and the southern fire (dakṣiṇāgni).
Wal_3.33 There are three bases of meritorious action: that consisting of giving, that consisting of ethical discipline, and that consisting of cultivation.
There are three modes of rebirth in the realm of desire (*kāmopapatti*). What are the three?

There are beings for whom sensual pleasures are present, who exercise sovereignty and control over those present sensual pleasures; such as humans and certain gods. This is the first mode of rebirth in the realm of desire.

There are beings whose desires are self-created, who, having created them repeatedly, exercise mastery over those created desires; such as the gods who Delight in Creations (*nirmāṇarati*). This is the second rebirth in the realm of desire.

There are beings whose desires are created by others, who, through desires created by others, exercise mastery over them; such as the gods who Wield Power over Creations (*paranirmitavaśavartin*). This is the third rebirth in the realm of desire.
Wal_3.35 Three ways of rebirth in happiness.
Wal_3.35.1.a There are beings who drench, steep, fill, and pervade this very body with the joy and happiness born of seclusion; there is no part of their entire body that is not suffused by it.
That which is to be pervaded is as follows: namely, by the joy and happiness born of seclusion.
By means of that happiness and that mental ease, they remain for a long time with a long lifespan, just like the gods of the Brahma-realm. This is the first rebirth in happiness.
There are beings who thoroughly moisten and completely drench this very body with the joy and happiness born of meditative concentration.
They fill and pervade [the body]; there is nothing whatsoever throughout the entire body that remains unpervaded by the joy and bliss born of concentration.
By means of that bliss and that mental happiness, they remain for a long time with a long life-span, just like the Ābhāsvara gods. This is the second rebirth in happiness.

There are beings who thoroughly drench, thoroughly soak, thoroughly fill, and thoroughly pervade this very body with a happiness free from rapture; there is no part of their entire body that is not pervaded by that happiness free from rapture.

By means of that happiness and that mental well-being, they remain for a long time with a long life-span, just like the Śubhakṛtsna deities. This is the third rebirth in happiness. (Wal 3.36) There are three kinds of wisdom: wisdom consisting of hearing, wisdom consisting of reflection, and wisdom consisting of cultivation.
(Wal 3.37) There are three kinds of wisdom: the wisdom of one in training, the wisdom of one beyond training, and the wisdom of neither-one-in-training-nor-beyond-training.

Wal_3.38 There are three faculties: the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known. Wal_3.39 There are three eyes: the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the wisdom eye.
Wal_3.40 There are three weapons: the weapon of learning, the weapon of seclusion, and the weapon of wisdom.
Wal_3.41 There are three trainings: the training in higher ethics, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.
Wal_3.42 There are three cultivations: the cultivation of ethics, the cultivation of concentration, and the cultivation of wisdom.
Wal_3.43 There are three abidings: the divine abiding, the sublime abiding, and the noble abiding.

Wal_3.44 There are three concentrations: concentration with applied thought and sustained thought; concentration without applied thought and with only sustained thought; concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought. Wal_3.45 There are three miracles: the miracle of psychic power, the miracle of mind-reading, and the miracle of instruction. Wal_3.46 There are three purities: purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind.
Wal_3.47 There are three forms of silence: silence of body, silence of speech, and silence of mind.
Wal_3.48 There are three sovereignties: sovereignty over the world, sovereignty over oneself, and sovereignty over the Dharma.
Wal_3.49 There are three unsurpassed qualities: the unsurpassed nature of knowledge, the unsurpassed nature of the path of practice, and the unsurpassed nature of liberation.

There are three types of knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣya-vidyā*). Which three? The knowledge of realization through the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-sākṣīkriyā*) belonging to one beyond training; the knowledge of realization through the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapāda-jñāna-sākṣīkriyā*) belonging to one beyond training; and the knowledge of realization through the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna-sākṣīkriyā*) belonging to one beyond training. Intermediate Summary Verse:
Training, cultivation,
and the masteries.
The three unsurpassed things...
the time, the fire of passion, and the training.
Venerable sirs, there are four things that have been proclaimed by the Blessed One after he himself realized them through direct knowledge and awakened to them:

namely, the four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four? They are the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body in the body; the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of feelings in feelings; the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the mind in the mind; and the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of phenomena in phenomena.
Having become united, harmonious, and living in concord, we shall [practice] as before, up to [the attainment of the goal] for gods and humans.

Wal_4.2.1 The four right efforts. Which four? He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, takes hold of the mind, and strives for the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have already arisen.
Wal_4.2.2 He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, takes hold of the mind, and strives for the non-arising of evil, unwholesome states that have not yet arisen.

Wal_4.2.3 For the arising of unarisen wholesome states, he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, takes hold of the mind, and strives. Wal_4.2.4 For the stability, non-confusion, cultivation, fulfillment, increase, expansion, and realization through knowledge of arisen wholesome states, he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, and takes hold of the mind.
He exerts himself and applies himself.
There are four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). Which four?
The base of psychic power endowed with the concentration of desire and the formative forces of abandonment (*chandasamādhiprahāṇasaṃskārasamanvāgata-ṛddhipāda*).

The basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of exertion and concentration of energy; the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of exertion and concentration of mind;
the basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of exertion and concentration of investigation.

The four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). Which four? Here, venerable friends, a monk, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first meditative absorption, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

Furthermore, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a monk enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and possesses the joy and happiness of internal serenity and mental unification. Furthermore, with the fading away of joy, a monk dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware, and experiences happiness.
He experiences it with the body; that which the Noble Ones describe as "dwelling in happiness, mindful and equanimous"—having attained and dwelling in this third dhyāna, which is free from joy.
Furthermore, a monk, through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of mental ease and distress...
With the subsiding of [the previous stages], he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.

The Four Noble Truths: What are the four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
The Four Perceptions: What are the four? Some perceive the limited; some perceive the vast; some perceive the immeasurable; and some perceive that "there is nothing at all."
Thus some perceive the sphere of nothingness.
There are four immeasurables. Which four? The immeasurable of loving-kindness, the immeasurable of compassion, the immeasurable of sympathetic joy, and the immeasurable of equanimity.
There are four formless attainments. Which four?

"Venerable ones, here a monk, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking 'space is infinite,' enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space, just as the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite space."

Furthermore, monks, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, [a monk] dwells having attained the sphere of infinite consciousness, just as the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite consciousness. Furthermore, monks, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, [a monk] dwells having attained the sphere of nothingness, thinking "there is nothing at all," just as the gods [who have reached the sphere of nothingness].

Those who have reached the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatanopaga*). Furthermore, a monk, having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, dwells having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), just like the gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, a monk delights in abandonment, is devoted to the practice of delighting in abandonment, delights in cultivation, and is devoted to the practice of delighting in cultivation.

He is devoted to it. Indeed, by that delight in abandonment and delight in cultivation... whoever therein is skillful, untiring, clearly comprehending, and mindful, he is said to be established in the ancient lineage of the noble ones.
Wal_4.10.a There are four fruits of asceticism. Which four? The fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the supreme fruit, arhatship.
4.10.b // Summary Verse //
… the formless attainments, the noble lineages, and the fruits.
Wal_4.11 There are four factors of stream-entry. Which four? Associating with superior persons, hearing the true Dharma, appropriate attention, and practice in accordance with the Dharma.

Wal_4.12 One who has entered the stream is endowed with four factors: he is possessed of verified confidence in the Buddha, verified confidence in the Dharma, verified confidence in the Saṅgha, and [the precepts] beloved by the noble ones.
Endowed with the ethical precepts (śīla).

There are four knowledges (jñāna). Which four? Knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), knowledge of the minds of others (paracitta-jñāna), and conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna).

There are four knowledges. Which four? Knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), knowledge of the origin (samudaya-jñāna), knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), and knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna).
Wal 4.15 There are four powers. Which four? The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.
Wal 4.16 There are four foundations. Which four? The foundation of wisdom, the foundation of truth, the foundation of relinquishment, and the foundation of tranquility.
Wal 4.17 There are four aggregates of dharma. Which four? The aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, and the aggregate of liberation.

There are four supports. What are the four? One practices certain dharmas after careful consideration; one endures certain dharmas after careful consideration; one avoids certain dharmas after careful consideration; one dispels certain dharmas after careful consideration. There are four dharma-footings. What are the four? Non-violence is a dharma-footing; non-malice is a dharma-footing; right mindfulness is a dharma-footing; and right concentration is a dharma-footing.

There are four qualities to be realized. There are qualities to be realized by means of the body; there are qualities to be realized by means of mindfulness; there are qualities to be realized by means of vision; and there are qualities to be realized by means of wisdom. Summary verse:
The factors of one who has entered the stream are the factors of one who has gone into the stream;
... knowledge.
... likewise.
The bases, the aggregates, the supports, and the steps—
these four things to be realized constitute the section that has been fully set forth.
Wal_4.21 There are four elements. Which four? The earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.

Wal_4.22 There are four nutriments. Which four? Edible food, whether gross or subtle; second, contact; third, mental volition; and fourth, consciousness. Wal_4.23 There are four stations of consciousness: the station of consciousness associated with form, the station of consciousness associated with feeling, the station of consciousness associated with perception, and the station of consciousness associated with formations.

Wal_4.24 There are four arisings of craving. Craving arises in a monk or a nun on account of robes; ... craving, becoming attached, becomes firmly attached. Likewise, craving arises in a monk or a nun on account of alms-food, on account of lodgings, and on account of existence and non-existence; craving, becoming attached, becomes firmly attached.

Wal 4.25. There are four ways of going to a wrong course. What are the four? One goes to a wrong course out of desire; one goes to a wrong course out of hatred, delusion, or fear. Wal 4.26. There are four ways of answering questions: a question to be answered categorically; a question to be answered by way of analysis; a question to be answered with a counter-question; and a question to be set aside. Wal 4.27. There are four purifications of offerings: there is an offering that is purified by the giver, not by the recipient.
There is that which is purified by the recipient and not by the donor; there is that which is purified neither by the donor nor by the recipient;
and there is the gift that is purified both by the donor and by the recipient.
The four bases of sympathy (*saṃgrahavastu*) are: generosity (*dāna*), pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*), purposeful action (*arthacaryā*), and consistency of purpose (*samānārthatā*).
Wal_4.29 There are four modes of birth. Which four? Birth from an egg, birth from a womb, birth from moisture, and spontaneous birth.

Wal_4.30 There are four ways of acquiring an individual existence (*ātmabhāva*). There is an acquisition of individual existence in which one's own volition prevails, but not the volition of another; there is an acquisition of individual existence in which the volition of another prevails, but not one's own volition.

There is an acquisition of personal existence in which one's own volition operates, but not the volition of another; there is an acquisition of personal existence in which neither one's own volition nor the volition of another operates. Summary verse: …
These ten are [attained] by means of the personal existence (ātmabhāva).

Wal_4.31 There are four modes of practice (*pratipad*). Which four? The painful mode of practice with slow direct knowledge; the painful mode of practice with quick direct knowledge; the pleasant mode of practice with slow direct knowledge; and the pleasant mode of practice with quick direct knowledge. Wal_4.32 There are four modes of practice: the unendurable mode of practice, the taming mode of practice, the patient mode of practice, and the peaceful mode of practice.

There are four cultivations of concentration. There is a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life. There is a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision. There is a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to the penetration of wisdom.
There is a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to the destruction of the taints.

Wal 4.34 There are four types of action: there is black action with black ripening; there is white action with white ripening; there is black-and-white action with black-and-white ripening; and there is action that is neither black nor white, with neither black nor white ripening.
It conduces to the exhaustion of karma.
There are four ways of undertaking dharma. There is an undertaking of dharma that is pleasant in the present but results in suffering in the future.
There is an undertaking of dharma that is pleasant in the present and results in happiness in the future. There is an undertaking of dharma...

There is an undertaking of dharmas that is painful in the present and results in suffering in the future; there is an undertaking of dharmas that is pleasant in the present and results in happiness in the future. There are four yokes: the yoke of sensual desire, the yoke of existence, the yoke of views, and the yoke of ignorance.

Wal_4.37 There are four dissociations: dissociation from the yoke of sensual desire, dissociation from the yoke of existence, dissociation from the yoke of views, and dissociation from the yoke of ignorance. Wal_4.38 There are four floods: the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance.
Wal_4.39 There are four clingings: clinging to sensual desire, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, and clinging to the doctrine of self.
There are four bodily ties: the bodily tie of covetousness, ill will, adherence to rules and observances, and the bodily tie of dogmatic insistence on "this alone is the truth."
The summary verse:
...and also the cultivation of the practice of concentration.
Karma, the undertaking of dharmas, as well as application and dissociation.
The flood, the clinging, and the tie—this is declared to be the group [of chapters].

Wal 4.41: There are four types of persons: the person who goes with the stream, the person who goes against the stream, the person who stands firm, and the person who has crossed over, gone to the further shore, and stands on dry land.

Wal_4.42 There are four types of persons: there is the person who is practicing for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others; there is the person who is practicing for the benefit of others but not for his own benefit; there is the person who is practicing neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others;
and there is the person who is practicing both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others.

Wal_4.43 There are four types of persons: there is the person who goes from darkness to darkness; there is the person who goes from darkness to light; there is the person who goes from light to darkness; and there is the person who goes from light to light. Wal_4.44 There are four types of persons: there is the person who torments themselves, devoted to the practice of self-mortification; there is the person who...
There is a person who is a scorcher of others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others;

there is a person who is neither a scorcher of others nor devoted to the practice of tormenting others, and neither a scorcher of self nor devoted to the practice of tormenting self; and there is a person who is both a scorcher of self, devoted to the practice of tormenting self, and a scorcher of others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others.

He does not practice self-mortification nor is he devoted to the practice of self-torment; he does not mortify others nor is he devoted to the practice of tormenting others... (Wal_4.45) There are four types of verbal misconduct: false speech, slander, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter.
(Wal_4.46) There are four types of verbal good conduct: abstaining from false speech, abstaining from slander, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from frivolous chatter.

Wal_4.47 There are four ignoble modes of discourse: claiming to have seen what was not seen is an ignoble mode of discourse; claiming to have heard what was not heard; claiming to have thought what was not thought; and claiming to have cognized what was not cognized is an ignoble mode of discourse. Wal_4.48 There are four noble modes of discourse: claiming not to have seen what was not seen is a noble mode of discourse; claiming not to have heard what was not heard; claiming not to have thought what was not thought; and claiming not to have cognized what was not cognized is a noble mode of discourse.

Wal_4.49 There are four ignoble modes of discourse: claiming not to have seen what was seen is an ignoble mode of discourse; claiming not to have heard what was heard; claiming not to have thought what was thought; claiming not to have cognized what was cognized is an ignoble mode of discourse. Wal_4.50 There are four noble modes of discourse: claiming to have seen what was seen is a noble mode of discourse; claiming to have heard what was heard; claiming to have thought what was thought; claiming to have cognized what was cognized is a noble mode of discourse.
Wal_5.1 Venerable ones, there are five qualities that have been declared by the Blessed One after having personally realized and fully awakened to them through direct knowledge.

Namely, the five aggregates: the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness. Having become united, harmonious, and living in concord, we [should practice] as before, up to [the attainment of] gods and humans. (Wal_5.2) The five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandhāḥ*). Which five? The aggregate of clinging to form, clinging to feeling, clinging to perception, clinging to mental formations, and clinging to consciousness.

The five strands of sensual pleasure: forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; sounds cognizable by the ear that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust;
odors cognizable by the nose that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; [tastes cognizable by the tongue...]

Flavors that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing in form, connected with sensual desire, and gratifying; tangible objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing in form, connected with sensual desire, and gratifying.

(Wal_5.4) There are five types of stinginess: stinginess regarding dwellings, stinginess regarding families, stinginess regarding physical appearance, stinginess regarding gains, and stinginess regarding the Dharma.

Wal 5.5 There are five destinies: the destiny of hell-beings, the destiny of animals, the destiny of hungry ghosts, the destiny of humans, and the destiny of gods. Wal 5.6 There are five hindrances. Which five? The hindrance of sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.

Wal 5.7 There are five mental wastelands. Which five? Here, venerable sirs, a monk is hesitant and doubtful regarding the Teacher; he does not enter into it, does not resolve upon it, and does not gain serene confidence in it.
And when wise fellow-celibates urge him with the goads of their words, he wavers, hesitates, does not leap forward, does not resolve, and does not become serene.

(Wal_5.8.1.a) There are five mental fetters. What are the five? Here, venerable friends, a monk is not free from passion for the body, not free from desire, not free from affection, not free from thirst, and not free from craving for it.

Wal_5.8.1.b That monk who has not yet become free from passion for the body—as described previously—his mind does not enter into it, does not become serene, does not settle, and does not resolve itself toward the application of exertion, toward abandonment, and toward the attainment of the supreme goal. Wal_5.8.1.c His mind does not enter [into it], as before, for the sake of attaining the supreme goal. Thus, this is his first mental bond.
Furthermore, monks, a monk who has not yet abandoned passion for sensual pleasures, who has not abandoned desire, affection, thirst,
and craving for them— just as before— that monk’s mind does not enter into, does not become clear toward, does not settle in, and does not resolve upon ardent application, exertion,
and striving for the attainment of the supreme goal.

His mind does not leap forward toward the attainment of the supreme goal, as previously described; thus, this is his second mental bond. Furthermore, a monk dwells in association with others... rejoicing in their joys and grieving in their sorrows; he is happy when they are happy and miserable when they are miserable;
and when tasks or duties arise, he applies himself to them personally.

Wal_5.8.3.b That monk who dwells in social intimacy, as described before, finds that his mind does not incline toward, does not become serene in, does not settle in, and does not resolve upon application, exertion, abandonment, and the attainment of the supreme goal. Wal_5.8.3.c His mind does not incline [toward the supreme goal], as previously described, for the attainment of the supreme goal. Thus, this is his third mental bond.
Furthermore, monks, there is a discourse that leads to seclusion, to the removal of mental hindrances, and to the attainment of the goal— namely,

a discourse on ethical discipline, a discourse on concentration, a discourse on wisdom, a discourse on liberation, a discourse on the knowledge and vision of liberation, a discourse on fewness of desires, a discourse on contentment, a discourse on solitude,
a discourse on non-association, and a discourse on relinquishment. [In such matters] he does not wish to listen, nor does he lend an ear.

He does not lend an ear; he does not apply his mind to understanding; he acts in violation of the Dharma that accords with the Dharma, transgressing the Teacher’s instruction… (Wal_5.8.4.b) That monk who, regarding this discourse on effacement—as previously described—does not desire to hear it, does not lend an ear, does not apply his mind to understanding, and acts in violation of the Dharma that accords with the Dharma…
The teaching of the Teacher continues...
his mind does not leap forward, as before, for the sake of attaining the supreme goal. Thus, this is his fourth mental bond...
Furthermore, a monk [is satisfied] with a mere trifling, a mere inferior attainment of distinction...

Wal_5.8.5.b Even with a slight and inferior degree of attainment of distinction, he does not fall into negligence in the interval, but applies himself to ardor, devotion, and exertion for the sake of attaining the supreme goal.

Wal_5.8.5.c Yet his mind does not leap forward toward the attainment of the supreme goal, as previously described. Thus, this is his fifth mental bond. Wal_5.9 There are five lower fetters: sensual desire, ill will, the view of a self-identity, adherence to rules and observances, and doubt.
Wal 5.10 There are five fetters pertaining to the higher [realms]: attachment to the realm of form, attachment to the formless realm, restlessness, conceit, and ignorance.

Wal 5.13 There are five calamities: the calamity of relatives, the calamity of wealth, the calamity of health, the calamity of virtue, and the calamity of view. Wal 5.14 There are five perfections: perfection of relatives, perfection of wealth, perfection of health, perfection of virtue, and perfection of view.

Wal 5.15 Five kinds of speech: those spoken at the proper time and those spoken at the improper time; those that are true and those that are untrue; those connected with the goal and those not connected with the goal. Wal 5.16 Five states of incapacity: An Arhat monk whose outflows are exhausted is incapable of intentionally depriving a living being of life; he is incapable of taking what is not given, which constitutes theft; he is incapable of engaging in sexual intercourse.
It is impossible for one who is fully conscious to speak falsely... There are five factors of one who exerts himself.
Here, a monk has faith established in the Tathāgata, rooted and firmly grounded... according to the nature of things (*dharmatā*). This is the first factor of one who exerts himself.
Furthermore, a monk [is endowed with] fellow practitioners of the holy life. This is the second factor of excellence.

Furthermore, a monk is free from illness, of a healthy constitution, and possesses a digestive system that is well-balanced—not too hot, not too cold, untroubled, and pleasant for the seasons—by which he properly and comfortably digests what he has eaten, drunk, and chewed.
They reach full maturity; this is the third factor of one who is preeminent.
Furthermore, a monk... is powerful... firm in his exertion, not casting off the burden regarding wholesome qualities.
"Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain; let the body wither away, along with flesh and blood; yet..."
Furthermore, that which is to be attained by one who has initiated vigor— one who is steadfast, vigorous, energetic, firm in prowess,
and who does not cast off the burden regarding wholesome qualities— alas, let there be no slackening of vigor before it is reached.
This is the fourth factor of the preeminent person.

Wal_5.18 There are five perceptions that ripen for liberation: the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, the perception of non-self in what is suffering, the perception of repulsiveness in food, and the perception of death.
Wal_5.19 There are five bases of liberation. What are the five?
Wal_5.19.1.a Here, monks, the Teacher teaches the Dharma, or some wise fellow practitioner who occupies the position of a teacher.

In whatever way his teacher, or any other wise companion in the holy life who stands in the position of a guru, teaches the Dharma to him, in that very way he comes to experience the meaning and experiences the Dharma within those teachings. As he experiences the meaning and experiences the Dharma, joy arises; for one who is joyful, rapture arises.

For one whose mind is joyful, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one experiences happiness; for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated; with a concentrated mind, one knows things as they truly are and sees things as they truly are; knowing things as they truly are and seeing things as they truly are, one becomes disenchanted; being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate; being dispassionate, one is liberated. This is...
The first basis of liberation: wherein,
for a monk or a nun who abides [in this], unestablished mindfulness becomes established,
the unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated, the unabandoned outflows are abandoned, and the unsurpassed security from bondage not yet attained is attained.
One attains nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, monk, it may be that neither the Teacher nor some other wise person standing in the position of a guru or fellow-celibate teaches the Dharma;
rather, one [attains it] by means of the teachings as they were heard, as they were instructed, and as they were mastered in detail.
He recites the study aloud.

To the extent that he recites those [teachings] aloud in detail—exactly as they were heard, exactly as they were taught, and exactly as they were mastered—to that same extent he comes to experience the meaning within them, as described before. This is the second base of liberation.

"Abiding therein," as before. Furthermore, monk, it may be that neither the Teacher nor some other wise person standing in the position of a teacher or a fellow-celibate teaches the Dharma; rather, one [teaches] the Dharmas exactly as they were heard, exactly as they were instructed, and exactly as they were mastered, in detail.
He practices recitation; moreover, he elucidates in detail for others those teachings as they were heard, as they were taught, and as they were mastered—
just as those teachings were heard, as they were taught, and as they were mastered, he elucidates them in detail for others.
He elucidates them in such a way that he becomes one who experiences the meaning within those phenomena, as described previously.
This is the third base of liberation (*vimuktyāyatana*), wherein one who is established [attains realization], as described previously.

Furthermore, O monk, it is not that the Teacher [is present] as before, nor does he recite [the teachings] himself, nor does he elucidate them to others; rather, [one understands] the teachings exactly as they were heard, up to exactly as they were mastered.
He reflects, weighs, and examines them.

In whatever way he reflects, and so forth, up to examining those teachings as they were heard and mastered, in that very way he experiences the meaning within those teachings, as described before. This is the fourth base of liberation.
"Abiding therein," as before.

Furthermore, O monk, it is not that he acts as a teacher, as before; nor does he recite [the scriptures], nor does he explain them to others, nor does he reflect upon them. Rather, by means of this, he thoroughly and correctly attends to some auspicious sign of concentration (*samādhinimitta*).
It is well-grasped, well-attended to, well-cultivated, well-practiced, and well-penetrated— just as [the perception of] a livid corpse,
or a festering corpse, or a bloated corpse, or a fissured corpse, or a blood-stained corpse, or a devoured corpse, or a scattered corpse,
or a skeleton, or a chain of bones.

In whatever way he has thoroughly penetrated any one or another of the auspicious signs of concentration, as previously described, in that very way he becomes one who experiences the meaning (*arthapratisaṃvedī*) regarding those phenomena, as previously described. This is the fifth basis of liberation (*vimuktyāyatana*), wherein, as before, for one who is established...
The five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*). Which five? The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
The five faculties. Which five? The faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of mental joy, the faculty of mental grief, and the faculty of equanimity.
The five powers (*pañca balāni*). Which five? The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.

Wal_5.22 There are five who do not return [to this world]. Which five? One who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state; one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth; one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion; one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion; and one who goes upstream (ūrdhvasrotas). Wal_5.23 There are five Pure Abodes: the Avṛhas, the Atapas, the Sudṛśas, the Sudarśanas, and the Akaniṣṭhas.
Wal_5.24 There are five elements leading to deliverance. For that noble disciple, O Venerable Ones, who has heard much... [regarding] sensual desires...

For one who recollects sensual pleasures, the mind does not enter into them, does not find clarity in them, does not settle upon them, is not liberated from them, but recoils; just as a bundle of sinews cast into a fire recoils and does not... for one who recollects sensual pleasures, the mind does not enter into them, does not find clarity in them, does not settle upon them, is not liberated from them, but recoils.
He does not experience that feeling; this is the escape.

As it is with sensual desires, so it is with ill-will and non-ill-will, harmfulness and non-harmfulness, form and the formless, the view of a personal identity and the cessation of the view of a personal identity—there is an escape.
Summary verse: ...
It is so: ...
and the barren wastes as well as the fetters ...
/ ... the ripening for liberation ...
Likewise, the second faculty, the five powers, the non-returner, and the pure abode realms.
Venerable friends, there are six things that have been proclaimed by the Blessed One after he had personally realized and fully awakened to them:
namely, the six internal sense bases (*āyatana*). Which six? The eye as an internal sense base; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as internal sense bases.
Having become united, harmonious, and living in mutual concord, we shall [practice] as before, up until [the attainment of] gods and humans.

There are six external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*). Which six? Visible form is an external sense base; sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena (*dharma*) are external sense bases. There are six groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*). Which six? Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. There are six groups of contact (*sparśakāya*). Which six? Eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact.

There are six groups of feeling (*vedanākāya*). Which six? Feeling born of eye-contact; feeling born of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact. There are six groups of perception (*saṃjñākāya*). [Which six? Perception born of eye-contact; perception born of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact.
There are six groups of volition (*cetanākāya*). Which six? Volition born of eye-contact; volition born of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact.
Wal_6.8 There are six groups of craving (*tṛṣṇākāya*). Which six? Craving born of eye-contact; craving born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.

Wal_6.9 There are six qualities conducive to decline (*hānabhāgīya*). Which six? One dwells without respect for the Buddha; one dwells without respect for the Dharma; one dwells without respect for the Saṅgha; one dwells without respect for the training; and one is difficult to speak with.
And one becomes a bad friend. There are six qualities conducive to distinction. What are the six? One dwells with reverence for the Buddha; one dwells with reverence for the Dharma;
one dwells with reverence for the Saṅgha; one dwells with reverence for the training; and one is easy to speak to and possesses a virtuous friend.

Wal_6.11 There are six applications of mental joy (*saumanasyopavicāra*). Which six? Having seen forms with the eye, one applies the mind to forms that are a basis for joy; having heard sounds with the ear, one applies the mind to sounds that are a basis for joy;
having smelled odors with the nose, one applies the mind to odors that are a basis for joy; [having tasted] flavors with the tongue...

Having tasted flavors conducive to mental pleasure, one dwells upon them; having touched tangible objects with the body, one dwells upon those tangible objects conducive to mental pleasure; having cognized mental phenomena with the mind, one dwells upon those mental phenomena conducive to mental pleasure.
There are six modes of dwelling upon mental displeasure. Which six? Having seen forms with the eye, [those] conducive to mental displeasure...
One dwells upon forms; having heard sounds with the ear, one dwells upon sounds that are a basis for mental distress;

having smelled odors with the nose, one dwells upon odors that are a basis for mental distress; having tasted flavors with the tongue, one dwells upon flavors that are a basis for mental distress; having touched tangibles with the body, [one dwells upon tangibles] that are a basis for mental distress.
One dwells upon tangibles. Having cognized mental objects with the mind, one dwells upon those mental objects that are a basis for dejection.

There are six modes of dwelling in equanimity. Which six? Having seen forms with the eye, one dwells upon forms that are a basis for equanimity. Having heard sounds with the ear, one dwells upon sounds that are a basis for equanimity. With the nose...

Having smelled odors that are conducive to equanimity, one dwells upon those odors with equanimity; having tasted flavors with the tongue that are conducive to equanimity, one dwells upon those flavors with equanimity; having touched tangibles with the body that are conducive to equanimity, one dwells upon those tangibles with equanimity;
having cognized mental phenomena with the mind that are conducive to equanimity, one dwells upon those phenomena with equanimity.

Wal_6.14.1 There are six constant abidings. What are the six? Here, a monk, having seen forms with the eye, is neither glad nor sad; he abides in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending. Wal_6.14.2 Having heard sounds with the ear, smelled odors with the nose, tasted flavors with the tongue, touched tangibles with the body, or cognized mental phenomena with the mind, he is neither glad nor sad; he abides in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
Wal_6.15 There are six elements. Which six? The earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.

Wal_6.16 There are six elements conducive to deliverance. Which six? Here, venerable friends, a monk might say: "I have cultivated, developed, and frequently practiced the meditative concentration of a mind of loving-kindness, yet nevertheless, ill will continues to overwhelm my mind."
It remains as before, as in the *Daśottara-sūtra*.
There are six roots of dispute. What are the six?
Here, a certain person is prone to anger and resentment. Being one who is prone to anger and resentment, he [speaks ill] of the Teacher...

He does not honor, revere, respect, or worship [the Teacher]. By not honoring, revering, respecting, or worshipping the Teacher, he does not see the Dharma. Not seeing the Dharma, he becomes indifferent toward the state of a recluse (*śrāmaṇya*). One who is indifferent toward the state of a recluse produces such quarreling, brawling, strife, and dispute within the Saṅgha.
Whoever is a creator of strife will bring about the misfortune, the harm, and the suffering of many people;
he will bring about misfortune, harm, and suffering for gods and humans alike.
Therefore, when you perceive such a root of dispute—whether internal or external—to be unabandoned, [you should strive to abandon it].

Then, being united, complete, and rejoicing without dispute, you should apply yourselves with intense enthusiasm, exertion, indefatigability, and non-opposition, through mindfulness and clear comprehension. In this way, that root of dispute which has arisen is abandoned.
Therefore, you should clearly perceive such a root of dispute as it arises, whether internally or externally, so that it may be abandoned.

Then, being united, complete, and rejoicing without dispute, one should, with intense mindfulness as a protection of the mind, practice yoga through heedfulness. ... [Otherwise] a great [suffering] will arise in the future.
Just as one who is prone to anger and resentment becomes so, so too does one who is deceitful, malicious, envious, stingy, treacherous, or hypocritical.

“Wrong view… adherence to one’s own views, grasping at what is improper, and being difficult to release…” Whatever monk is one who adheres to his own views, grasps at what is improper, and is difficult to release… he does not honor the Teacher,
and so on as before, up to: “it will not arise in the future.”

Wal_6.18 There are six qualities that promote cohesion. Which six? "May my bodily action toward the Teacher and toward wise fellow-practitioners be established as friendly"—this is a quality that promotes cohesion, as previously described in the *Daśottara*.

Wal_6.19 There are six higher knowledges (*abhijñā*). Which six? The domain of supernormal power, the divine ear, knowledge of the minds of others, recollection of past lives, knowledge of death and rebirth, and the destruction of the taints (*āsravakṣaya*).

Wal_6.20 There are six perceptions conducive to clear knowledge (*vidyābhāgīya*). What are the six? The perception of impermanence regarding the impermanent, the perception of suffering regarding what is suffering, the perception of non-self regarding what is not-self, the perception of repulsiveness regarding food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, and the perception of death. Wal_6.21 There are six recollections (*anusmṛti*): recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of ethical discipline (*śīla*), recollection of generosity (*tyāga*), and recollection of the deities (*devatā*).

Wal_6.22 There are six unsurpassables: the unsurpassability of seeing, the unsurpassability of hearing, the unsurpassability of gain, the unsurpassability of training, the unsurpassability of service, and the unsurpassability of recollection.
Wal_6.23 There are six examinations: examination of forms, examination of sounds, examination of odors, examination of tastes, examination of tangibles, and examination of mental phenomena.
Wal_6.24 There are six noble lineages. What are the six? A person of black lineage is born into black phenomena.
A person of black lineage gives birth to white phenomena; a person of black lineage gives birth to nirvana, which is neither black nor white. A person of white lineage gives birth to black phenomena;
a person of white lineage gives birth to white phenomena. A person of white lineage [gives birth to] that which is neither black...
The non-white [state], nirvāṇa, is fully realized.
// Summary Verse //
The internal and external [bases], consciousness, contact, feeling, perception, volition, and the elements...
… and disputes.
The six means of unification have been taught, and the six superknowledges have been revealed: perception, mindfulness, unsurpassedness, discernment, and noble birth.
Venerable ones, there are seven qualities that have been declared by the Blessed One, having realized them for himself through direct knowledge and full awakening;

namely, the seven factors of enlightenment. What are the seven? They are the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.
Having become united, harmonious, and living in mutual agreement, we shall [practice] as before, up until [the attainment of] gods and humans.

Namely, the seven types of persons: the follower by faith, the follower by Dharma, the one resolved through faith, the one who has attained vision, the body-witness, the one liberated through wisdom, and the one liberated both ways.
The seven requisites for concentration. What are the seven? Namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right mindfulness.

Wal_7.4 There are seven riches: the riches of faith, ethical discipline, moral shame, dread of blame, learning, relinquishment, and wisdom. Wal_7.5 There are seven powers: the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of moral shame, the power of dread of blame, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.
Wal_7.6 There are seven unwholesome qualities: one is lacking in faith, lacks moral shame, lacks dread of blame, is indolent, has muddled mindfulness, is unconcentrated, and is of poor wisdom.

Wal_7.7 There are seven true qualities: one is endowed with faith, possesses a sense of shame, possesses dread of blame, has aroused energy, is established in mindfulness, is concentrated, and is possessed of wisdom.

Wal_7.8 There are seven false qualities: one does not know the Dharma, does not know the meaning, does not know the proper time, does not know moderation, does not know oneself, does not know the assembly, and does not know the superior and inferior qualities of individuals. Wal_7.9 There are seven true qualities: one knows the Dharma, knows the meaning, knows the proper time, knows moderation, knows oneself, knows the assembly, and knows the superior and inferior qualities of individuals.

Wal_7.10 There are seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). There are sentient beings possessing form who are diverse in body and diverse in perception, such as human beings and certain gods. This is the first station of consciousness, as previously described in the *Daśottara-sūtra*. Wal_7.11 There are seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*): the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), the underlying tendency of aversion (*pratigha*), the underlying tendency of lust for existence (*bhavarāga*), the underlying tendency of pride (*māna*), the underlying tendency of ignorance (*avidyā*), the underlying tendency of views (*dṛṣṭi*), and the underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Wal_7.12 There are seven faultless matters (*nirdoṣavastu*), as previously [stated] in the *Daśottara-sūtra*.

Wal_7.13 There are seven methods for settling legal disputes (*adhikaraṇaśamatha*): face-to-face resolution (*saṃmukhavinaya*), resolution through recollection (*smṛtivinaya*), resolution for one who is no longer deluded (*amūḍhavinaya*), investigation into the nature of the offense (*tatsvabhāvaiṣīya*), majority decision (*yadbhūyasikīya*), formal confession (*pratijñākāraka*), and the "covering over with grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*).
Here is the summary verse (*uddāna*).

… seven persons, seven … true dharmas, seven … seven stations of consciousness, seven … seven faultless bases, seven [factors] of calm abiding … O Venerable Ones, eight dharmas have been proclaimed by the Blessed One, having realized them for himself through direct knowledge and full awakening.
Namely, the eight factors of the noble path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Being united, harmonious, and living in mutual agreement, we shall [practice them] as before, for the sake of gods and humans.

Wal_8.2 There are eight persons: the stream-enterer; the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry; the once-returner; the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning; the non-returner; the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning; the arhat; and the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of arhatship.

Wal_8.3 There are eight kinds of giving: one gives a gift out of proximity; one gives a gift out of fear; one gives a gift because [the recipient] has given to me; one gives a gift thinking, "He will give to me"; one gives a gift thinking, "This was given by my fathers and grandfathers in the past";
one gives a gift for the sake of heaven; one gives a gift for the sake of reputation; [and one gives] for the sake of adorning the mind and for the sake of equipping the mind.
One gives a gift for the sake of the equipment of yoga and for the attainment of the supreme goal.
There are eight bases of laziness and eight bases of meritorious action. Among these, the basis of meritorious action consisting of giving is when, in some cases, a small gift is given.

Wal_8.7 There are eight assemblies: the assembly of kṣatriyas, the assembly of brāhmaṇas, the assembly of householders, the assembly of śramaṇas, the assembly of the four great kings, the assembly of the thirty-three gods, the assembly of Māra, and the assembly of Brahmā.
Wal_8.8 There are eight worldly dharmas. Which eight? Gain, loss, blame, praise, fame, infamy, suffering, and happiness.
Wal_8.9 There are eight liberations.
Possessing form, one sees forms; this is the first liberation.
Being percipient of the internal as formless, one sees external forms; this is the second liberation.
Having personally realized the beautiful liberation with the body and having attained it, one dwells therein; this is the third liberation.

Furthermore, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, a monk enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space, [perceiving] "space is infinite. This is the fourth liberation.

Furthermore, a monk, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite space, attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is the fifth liberation. Furthermore, a monk, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing at all," attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness; this is the sixth [liberation].
Furthermore, a monk, having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, dwells having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the seventh liberation.

Furthermore, a monk, having completely transcended the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, dwells having personally realized and attained the cessation of perception and feeling; this is—
The eighth liberation.
The eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
(1) Perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are limited, beautiful or ugly; indeed, those...
Having mastered forms, one knows them; having mastered them, one sees them, and one possesses such a perception. This is the first sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Internally perceiving form, one sees external forms that are immeasurable, beautiful or ugly; having mastered those forms, one knows them; having mastered them, one sees them, and one possesses such a perception. This is the second sphere of mastery.

Wal_8.10.3 Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are limited, beautiful or ugly; having mastered those forms, one knows them, having mastered them, one sees them, and one has such a perception. This is the third base of mastery.
Wal_8.10.4 Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are immeasurable, beautiful or ugly; having mastered those [forms], one knows them...
Having mastered forms, one knows them; having mastered them, one sees them, and one possesses such a perception. This is the fourth base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Internally perceiving no form, one sees external forms that are blue, blue in color, appearing blue, and shining with blue light—just like the *umaka* flower, or a well-woven cloth from Vārāṇasī.

In the same way, one who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally that are blue, blue-colored, blue-appearing, and blue-luminous. Having mastered those forms, one knows them; having mastered them, one sees them. One becomes percipient in this way. This is the fifth base of mastery.

Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster, just like a blooming *karṇikāra* flower or a well-made cloth from Vārāṇasī.
In this very way, not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster.
They are yellow in radiance; having mastered those forms, he sees them and becomes percipient of them thus. This is the sixth base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Internally being percipient of the formless, he sees external forms that are red, of red color, appearing as red, and radiant with red light, just like a well-developed *bhaṇḍūka* flower.
Or like a Benares cloth;

even so, one who is percipient of the internal as formless sees external forms that are red, red in color, appearing red, and glowing red. Having mastered those forms, he sees them and becomes percipient in this way.
This is the seventh base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*):
being percipient of the formless internally, one sees external forms that are white, white in color, white in appearance, and white in luster— just like the star Venus,
or a well-washed cloth from Vārāṇasī.

In the same way, one who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally that are white, white in color, white in appearance, and white in luster; having mastered those forms, one sees them and is percipient in this way. This is the eighth base of mastery.
Venerable sirs, there are nine things proclaimed by the Blessed One after he had personally realized and fully awakened to them:
namely, the nine fetters— the fetter of attachment, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of pride, the fetter of ignorance,
the fetter of views, the fetter of grasping, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of envy, and the fetter of avarice.
Being united, harmonious, and living in mutual joy, we [shall proceed] as before, up to [the attainment of] gods and humans.
There are nine abodes of sentient beings. What are the nine?
There are sentient beings who possess form, diverse in body and diverse in perception, such as human beings and certain gods. This is the first abode of sentient beings.
Wal_9.2.2 There are material beings who are diverse in body and uniform in perception, such as the gods of the Brahma-group who were first produced. This is the second abode of beings.
Wal_9.2.3 There are material beings who are uniform in body and diverse in perception, such as the Ābhāsvara gods. This is the third abode of beings.
Wal_9.2.4 There are material beings who are uniform in body and uniform in perception, such as the Śubhakṛtsna gods. This is the fourth abode of beings.
There are beings with form who are without perception and without distinct perception; namely, the gods who are non-percipient beings. This is the fifth abode of beings.

There are beings without form who, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, having attained the base of infinite space through the thought "space is infinite," dwell therein.

For example, there are gods who have reached the sphere of infinite space; this is the sixth abode of beings. There are formless beings who, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite space, attain and dwell in the sphere of infinite consciousness; for example, the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is the seventh abode of beings.

There are formless beings who, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing whatsoever," dwell having attained the sphere of nothingness; such are the gods who have reached the sphere of nothingness. This is the eighth abode of beings.

“There are formless beings who, having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, dwell having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; namely, the gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is the ninth abode of beings.
“Venerable ones, there are ten qualities that have been declared by the Blessed One, having realized them for himself through direct knowledge and full awakening.”

Namely, the ten totalities (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*). Some perceive the earth-totality above, below, and across—non-dual and immeasurable. Others perceive the water-totality, the fire-totality, the wind-totality, the blue-totality, the yellow-totality, the red-totality, the white-totality, the space-infinity-totality, and the consciousness-infinity-totality.
Thus, above, below, and across, it is non-dual and immeasurable.

Being united and assembled, we [proclaim] as before, up to the gods and humans. (Wal_10.2) The ten qualities of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Which ten? The right view of one beyond training, right intention, right speech...

Right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, right liberation, and right knowledge. Then the Blessed One, having understood that the Venerable Śāriputra had finished speaking, sat down, crossed his legs, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him.

The Blessed One addressed the venerable Śāriputra: “Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra! It is indeed excellent that you, Śāriputra, have done so. Furthermore, you should repeatedly teach the *dharmaparyāya* known as the ‘Chanting Together’ (*saṃgīta*) to the monks. Let this be for the long-term benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. Monks, take up the *dharmaparyāya* ‘Chanting Together’ and retain it in such a way.”
Have it grasped; have it recited.

… [This] discourse on Dharma, connected with the holy life, conduces to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to Nirvana. And as long as this discourse on Dharma has been chanted out of faith by a true person who has gone forth, it should be taken up, mastered, and retained accordingly.
It should be caused to be grasped and it should be caused to be recited.
